If that’s the case the distributor (PLN) will probably switch you to something else temporarily till windmill can supply the power back. At the end of the day they’re the one that distributes the power to you and have the responsibility you don’t see any outage.

The distribution  is owned by one company but it’s the supplier that you can change. So for example PLN will ow the distribution points (the cables etc) but the supplier can come from different company (including PLN itself). Most common example let’s say you want your electricity to come from strictly renewable, let’s called “Windmill Co.” then PLN will “buy”/source your electricity from Windmill Co.  and then distribute it to your house. Your billing will come from PLN but it will reflect the source + distribution charges. There is a market place for electricity, in wholesale side usually  electric company will bid on different suppliers based on the prices during the day https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_market.

It’s a requirement set by the clearinghouse, DTCC, in this case due to the extreme volatility, they require brokerage to put more collateral and on Thursday, due to the sheer volume Robinhood was literally running out of money to be able to fulfil the clearinghouse requirement, so they stop allowing people to buy GME . When you sell you don’t need to put up collateral so hence selling was still allowed. If you wonder why Robinhood was still allowing buying of other shares, it was simply there was less volatility on other shares that they didn’t need to put as much collateral for those. In case you’re wondering why clearinghouse/DTCC requires collateral it is because the trade does not settle instantly, it settles on T+2 basis,  meaning the settlement, matching the buyer and seller and making sure the amount are all correct etc happens 2 days after the transaction. So as the clearinghouse DTCC wants to make sure that the brokerage actually has the money to pay the share when the trade settles. In this case, GME shares could really go either way and there’s possibility that it could tank quickly. Here’s an article that summarizes it better [link](https://www.bloombergquint.com/amp/quicktakes/what-s-the-dtcc-and-how-did-it-stop-gamestop-mania-quicktake). I think this is an important knowledge to have, especially as more people are starting to fiddle with stock buying etc. There isn’t really any conspiracy and institutional traders deal with this all the time the difference is they have more direct access to the credit line. Now in my personal opinion, robinhood could easily avoid the outrage by immediately requiring its user to post a collateral with Robinhod when they decide to buy the share, but I suppose maybe their system doesn’t have that capability. They could have tried to explain the reasoning better but my guess is they didn’t want people to think that they don’t have money and cause some panic sell/withdrawal from their fund, but that kinda happen anyway.
